rows.stem: Which arrow best shows the position of 11/3 on the number line?
rows.sourceEnglish: Which arrow best shows the position of 11/3 on the number line?

steps.reason: Divide the numerator 11 by the denominator 3 to convert the improper fraction 11/3 into a mixed number and repeating decimal.
Because 3⅔ is greater than 3 and less than 4, the point lies in the interval between 3 and 4, two-thirds of the way from 3 toward 4.
On the textbook number line, arrow C is just past 3 while arrow D is between 3 and 4 nearer to 4, so arrow D best represents 11/3.

rows.stem: Find any three rational numbers between -7/11 and 2/11.
rows.sourceEnglish: Find any three rational numbers between -7/11 and 2/11.

steps.reason: Both given rational numbers already share the same positive denominator 11, so we can compare them directly using their integer numerators.
Dividing each interior integer numerator by the common denominator 11 gives fractions strictly between −7/11 and 2/11.
Choose any three of these interior fractions, such as −6/11, −5/11, and −4/11.

rows.stem: Find any five rational numbers between

steps.reason: Convert both unit fractions to terminating decimals (or common-denominator fractions) and order the smaller bound 1/5 before the larger bound 1/4.
Pick five terminating decimals (or repeated arithmetic midpoints 9/40, 19/80, 39/160, 79/320, 159/640) strictly between 0.20 and 0.25.
Every terminating decimal is a rational number p/q, giving five valid rational numbers between 1/5 and 1/4.

rows.stem: Find any five rational numbers between

steps.reason: Append trailing zeros so both endpoints are written to three decimal places (thousandths) without changing their value.
Any thousandth from 0.101 up to 0.109 lies strictly between 0.100 and 0.110.
Select five distinct thousandths in that interval, such as 0.101, 0.102, 0.103, 0.104, and 0.105.

rows.stem: Find any five rational numbers between

steps.reason: On the number line, −2 lies to the left of −1, so −2 is the smaller endpoint and −1 is the larger endpoint.
Choose five terminating decimals (or repeated midpoints −3/2, −5/4, −9/8, −17/16, −33/32) strictly between −2 and −1.
List the five rational numbers inside the interval (−2, −1).
